# Authoring Anki flashcards
A card is a tool for one retrieval. If it asks for two things, it teaches neither. Everything below
follows from that.
Four targets, in priority order when they conflict: accurate, atomic, easy to recall, readable.
Accuracy wins over everything. A card that is memorable and wrong is worse than no card.
## Non-negotiable
Never write to the collection before showing the drafted cards and getting explicit approval.
Bad cards are expensive: they cost review time for months and are tedious to find and repair.
The approval table is the whole safety mechanism. Do not skip it, and do not treat "make me some
cards" as advance approval of specific cards.
Never invent facts to fill a card. If the source does not state it, the card does not exist.
When the source is thin or self-contradictory, say so and card only what it actually supports.
## Workflow
1. Read the source in full before writing anything. If you do not understand it, stop and say so
rather than carding it. Memorising something you do not understand produces unusable knowledge
(SuperMemo rules 1 and 2).
2. Run `python3 scripts/anki_cards.py check` from this skill's directory. If Anki is down,
offer to launch it with `open -a Anki`, then wait for AnkiConnect on port 8765. The check also
reports whether the skill's four note types are there. A missing one is created only after the
user approves, and one that differs is the user's to fix: see "Setting them up" in
`references/note-types.md`.
3. Write a fact inventory: one line per candidate fact, in plain text, before any card formatting.
Then cut. Most sources deserve 5 to 15 cards, not one per sentence. Cutting is the main quality
lever you have, so say out loud what you dropped and why. From code or API docs, mark each fact
with what the user will do with it: type it, read it, or decide with it (see Code below).
4. Pick the deck, the note type, and the `Topic` value. Run `anki_cards.py inspect "<deck>"` to see
what the deck already uses and to get real field names. Never guess field names. See
`references/note-types.md`. Cards learnt for a project, a client mission or a personal one, go
to `Inbox::<project>`. When the user asks for the Inbox, says the cards are not urgent, or no
current deck fits, the deck is `Inbox` (see "The Inbox" below). Never add to an archived deck, a
top-level deck whose name starts with `_`.
5. Draft to a JSON file in the scratchpad directory, one object per note. Shape:
`{"deckName": ..., "modelName": ..., "notes": [{"fields": {...}, "tags": [...]}]}`
6. Self-audit against the checklist below, then run
`anki_cards.py lint <draft.json>`. Fix every violation and re-lint until clean. The linter is
mechanical, so it catches slips but cannot judge whether a card is worth having. That is your job.
7. Show the cards as a table, get approval, then add with `mcp__anki__addNotes`, one call per
deck-and-model pair, at most 100 notes per call. Report what was created and what you left out.
## Rules
Atomicity and content:
- One card, one retrieval. A Front containing "and", "or", a slash, or two question marks is two cards.
- Prefer a question-and-answer card. Reach for cloze when the fact reads naturally as a sentence,
when you want both directions of an acronym or pairing, for a closed list, or to blank the line
that matters in a code snippet.
- Never ask for a set ("what are the five pillars"). Convert it into one cloze card per member, or
drop it. Listing members in a different order each review actively damages recall (SuperMemo 9).
- A procedure is an enumeration. Card what carries knowledge: the step people get wrong, the
condition that gates the next step, and why a step exists. Skip steps anyone doing the task would
infer. Asking for the whole sequence is an optional extra: one card for three steps or fewer
where each leads to the next, or, when a longer outline itself must be known, a cloze with one
index per step (SuperMemo 10).
- No yes-or-no and no true-or-false Fronts. A coin flip is not retrieval. Rephrase as an open question.
- No card whose answer is inferable from its own Front. If reading the question hands you the answer,
the card trains nothing.
- Ask "why" and "how" as well as "what". An explanation card holds better than a bare label, and
gives the fact something to hang on.
- Date-stamp volatile facts inside the card text: figures, versions, org charts, prices, headcounts.
Write "as of March 2026" in the card, not in the `Source`.
- Skip facts that are trivially derivable, that you would look up rather than recall, or that only
matter once.
Code, from source files, API docs, or a codebase the user works in:
- Card the use. A fact the user will type (a call, a command, a flag, a config key) gets a
production card: the Front states the goal with the names and values it needs, and the Back is
the code. Code they will read goes on the Front, asking what it returns, what it is for, or which
line is wrong. What they will decide with (why it is built this way, what must hold, what breaks)
gets a prose card with a one-reason answer. Neither kind trains the other, so mix them within a
topic rather than doing one first. When the user wants to write the code without looking it up,
most of their code cards ask for code, and each Front describes the situation they will be in
while coding: recalling a command when asked for it is not noticing when to use it.
- Size a code answer by what it holds. One line is the best-kept card. Up to six lines is fine when
they belong together, such as an idiom. Past six a review takes about twice as long, which is
worth paying for code the user writes again and again, a pattern or a task from their work: a
task card goes up to twelve lines, holds only the lines that make the pattern, ends with a
`Check:` line, and sits on top of cards for its key line and for when to use it. Inside a longer
snippet, blank the line that matters as a code cloze.
- Asking the user to write code, an example included, is the most direct practice for writing it.
The Front sets the task: the setting, the names, and what the code must do, or "of your choice"
when any example will do. The Back holds one solution, then a `Check:` line naming what every
correct answer contains, so a different correct solution passes. What fails is a bare "Write an
example of X" with one long answer to compare by eye, because nothing on the card says what
counts as right. For a pattern that matters, two or three task cards in different situations, or
one that leaves the example to the user, keep the review from turning into recall of one text.
- Card a call only when recalling it beats looking it up. Not what the editor completes, such as a
full import path.
- From a codebase, card what the code does not say: why it is written this way, what must hold,
where things live at module level, the path a request or a record takes, and the gotchas. Never a
verbatim implementation. The code is always there to re-read, and it changes under the card.
- A whole function, program, or algorithm problem is an exercise, not a Back. Anki can still
schedule it: offer a card that points to the exercise, written in an editor and checked against
tests, in a deck of its own, or the `Coding Exercises` note type if the user keeps an exercise
repository.
Phrasing:
- The Front never carries the `Topic` value as a label prefix. The note type renders it above the
question already, so `"Acme R&D: which committee ..."` is redundant. Naming the subject inside the
question is fine when it reads better, as in "What does `--frozen` do in `uv run`?".
- The `Topic` holds what you would already know when you need the fact: the tool you are working
in, or the subject you are thinking about. It never holds an answer, so it never names the tool
when the card asks which tool to use. If a Back or a cloze deletion equals it, widen it to the
subject the card belongs to (`Web APIs`, not `Fetch API`). Prefer a value many cards share: one
that only a handful of cards carry works as a hint.
- Shortest wording that stays unambiguous. Cut "What is the ...?" to the noun phrase when it reads
cleanly, and cut preamble that the Topic line already supplies.
- One unambiguous answer. If two answers are defensible, the Front is underspecified: add the
qualifier that picks one.
- Watch interference between sibling cards. When a source gives you six parallel items, near-identical
Fronts will blur together under review. Differentiate by the distinguishing content, or card only
the items that carry weight. Two Fronts that differ only in their `Topic` are the extreme case: put
the name that tells them apart in the question.
- Match the source language. A French source gets French cards.
Formatting, in full in `references/house-style.md`:
- Back is normally one short sentence ending in a period. A code Back is the code alone, with no
period: `<code>` for one line, `<pre><code>` for more, and a task card ends with its `Check:`
line.
- `<code>` for identifiers, flags, paths, and commands. `<i>` for a term being defined.
- No bold, no emoji, no em dash, no curly quotes, no bold-header bullet lists. Sources full of
emoji headings and bold (Confluence and Notion especially) must be stripped, not mirrored.
- Steps on a Back: two are one sentence joined with "then", such as `Add the package to

packages.yml, then run dbt deps.` Three are an `
    `, one short item
per step, each opening with its verb. Four or more are more than one card.
- `<ol>` also lays out a procedure inside a cloze Text, one cloze index per `<li>`, never running
across two items. Numbers assert order and count, so never use `<ol>` for a set, criteria, or
conditions.
- `<ul><li>` only for a closed list of two or three items that belongs on one card.
- Escape `<`, `>` and `&` inside code, or `List<String>` loses its `<String>`. In a cloze, a `::`
inside a deletion starts a hint, and a `}` just before the closing braces ends the deletion early.
- `Source` on every card: a link to the page the fact came from, with the page title as the link
text, such as `uv CLI reference`, or the
source in plain text when it has no URL.
- Tags: `client::<name>` on every card from client work, and `speed::fast` on every card the rule
in `references/house-style.md` marks quick to review. The linter applies that rule, so a request
never decides it. Nothing else is a tag: the subject is the `Topic`, the source is the `Source`,
and the kind of card is its note type.
## Self-audit before showing cards
Walk the drafted set once and ask:
1. The sigh test. Reading this Front cold, would you groan? A groan means it is too broad, too
ambiguous, or not worth remembering. Fix it or cut it.
2. Does any Front ask for two things?
3. Could any two cards in this batch be confused for each other?
4. Is every answer traceable to the page its `Source` names, with no inference of your own
presented as fact?
5. Does any Front repeat its own `Topic`, and does any `Topic` give away an answer?
6. Is any Back longer than it needs to be?
7. For each procedure, does the step that is easiest to get wrong have a card of its own?
8. Does every fact the user will type have a card that makes them produce it? Does every card that
asks for an example, and every Back over six lines of code, end with a `Check:` line?
9. Would you want this card in six months?
## Reviewing existing cards
When asked to critique or repair cards, fetch them with `mcp__anki__findNotes` and
`mcp__anki__notesInfo`, run the same audit, and report findings per note id with a concrete
rewrite for each. Apply changes with `mcp__anki__updateNoteFields` only after approval. Rewording a
field, such as making a list's items parallel, keeps the card's review history. Splitting a
bundled card means creating new notes and deleting the old one, which loses its review history, so
call that out and let the user decide. A card that asks for code to write usually stays one: give
its Front the task and its Back a `Check:` line, which are field edits that keep its history. A
long code Back becomes a task card cut to the lines that make the pattern, a production card for
the call that matters, or an exercise for a whole program (worked examples 10 and 11).
## Improving cards from their reviews
Reviews show which cards fail, which are slow, and which have gone out of date; reading cards cold
does not. `anki_cards.py candidates <kind>` picks them from the review history: `failing`, `slow`,
`sourced` or `random`. You diagnose each, draft one proposal, and `anki_cards.py queue add` keeps it
in a repair queue the user approves from later. Marking a note while reviewing, the `*` key, asks
for its repair. The `inbox` check also prints proposals a rule decides, ready to queue as they are:
the moves of learnt notes out of the Inbox, and the `speed::fast` changes its rule calls for.
- A run of a check never writes to the collection and asks nothing: it queues proposals, and records
a missed run when Anki is closed.
- When the user asks to go through the queue, show the approval table, apply what they approve as
above, and record every verdict with `anki_cards.py queue decide`.
Read `references/repair-queue.md` before running a check or going through the queue: what each
check picks, the diagnoses and their actions, the queue file, and how to run the checks on a
schedule.
## The Inbox
`Inbox` holds the cards still being learnt. A project, a client mission or a personal one, gets a
subdeck, `Inbox::<project>`, so that its cards can be studied as a set while the work lasts. Cards
with no project go to `Inbox` itself.
A card sent to the Inbox gets everything but its final deck: note type, `Topic`, `Source`, tags.
The `Topic` is what the card shows, and the deck never appears in review. A card from client work
also gets `client::<name>`, such as `client::acme`: client cards go only to a model the client has
cleared (`--no-client` in `references/repair-queue.md`), and once a card leaves its project deck
the tag is the only thing that still says so. A personal project's cards get no tag.
A note leaves the Inbox once it is learnt: every card of it has an interval of 21 days or more,
which Anki calls mature. It moves to the current deck holding the most cards with its `Topic`. When
no current deck does, the user names one, a broad category they study on its own, or keeps the note
with its project, and the Topic's later notes follow the deck they chose. Never move a note to an
archived deck, and never rebuild an archived tree.
The repair queue's `inbox` check proposes these moves every week. When the user asks to organize
the Inbox now:
1. Run `anki_cards.py inbox`. It groups the notes by `Topic` and says where cards with each one
live, marks the learnt notes, counts the overdue cards, shows each project deck's client tag,
and lists lint findings.
2. Propose one row per learnt note: the deck the rule gives, or, when it gives none, a broad deck
under a placeholder name for the user to name, or keeping the note with its project. Notes not
yet learnt stay where they are. Report a missing `Source` rather than guessing one. The source is
usually out of reach by now, so audit the form, and flag a doubtful fact instead of rewriting
it. A note that names its source in a tag instead gets that name moved into `Source` as plain
text, and the tag removed. Fixes follow "Reviewing existing cards" above.
3. Lead with what is decaying. Studied cards keep falling due, and a card that has waited more than
two weeks is losing the context it was written in.
4. After approval, apply fixes and new notes first, then tags with `mcp__anki__addTags` and
`mcp__anki__removeTags`, then move every card of each note with `mcp__anki__changeDeck`. Read the
card ids after the fixes, because a new cloze index makes a new card. A move keeps the card's
schedule and review history. Hand the user anything these tools cannot do, such as changing a
note type, and name any emptied project deck for them to delete.
## Reference files
Load these as needed rather than up front:
- `references/note-types.md`. The skill's four note types, defined in `assets/note-types.json` and
`assets/card.css`: their fields, how they render, which to pick, how to set up one that is missing
or older than its `Source` field, and the API traps that break a batch or drop a field. Read this
before choosing a note type.
- `references/house-style.md`. Formatting, HTML, the `Source` field, the two tags and the speed
rule, language, and the prose rules for card text. Read this before drafting.
- `references/principles.md`. The research canon with attribution. Read this when a judgement call
is genuinely unclear, for example how to handle an open-ended list, which parts of a procedure to
card, which facts from code deserve a code card, or whether two cards on one fact is redundancy or
waste.
- `references/worked-examples.md`. Before-and-after rewrites of real bad cards. Read this if the
rules above feel abstract, or to calibrate how short a good Back is.
- `references/repair-queue.md`. Finding the cards worth fixing from their reviews, the repair queue,
the weekly inbox check, and running the checks on a schedule. Read this before running a check or
going through the queue.

# House style for card text
Derived from real cards, plus the writing rules from the `humanizer` skill.
Cards are prose that gets read hundreds of times, so the writing rules matter more here than in
ordinary text, not less.
## Real cards
These are verbatim. They are the target.
Topic: uv
Front: What does the --frozen option do when using uv run?
Back:  Run without updating the lockfile.
Topic: Vim
Front: What is the difference between a temporary setting and a permanent setting in Vim?
Back: A temporary setting (e.g., :set number) is lost when Vim closes. A permanent setting is written to vimrc and persists across sessions.
Topic: Dagster
Front: Which tool is used to quickly scaffold a Python package containing a Dagster Definitions object?
Back: The create-dagster CLI.
Topic: Bot Detection
Front: Which tool uses the WebDriver protocol?
Back:  Selenium WebDriver.
Topic: Causal Inference
Front: Why can ML models not answer causal questions?
Back:  ML is about prediction and correlation, not causal structure. It cannot handle inverse causality, like low prices being associated with low hotel sales during off-season.
Topic: Finances publiques
Front: Qu'est-ce que les finances sociales ?
Back:  Ensemble des dépenses liées à la protection sociale et des ressources nécessaires à leur financement.
Note what is absent: no bold, no emoji, no em dash, no topic prefix in the Front, no multi-paragraph
Back, no "Note that", no headers inside a field.
## The context field, precisely
The rule is about label prefixes, not about the word appearing at all. These three Fronts all sit on
notes whose `Topic` is `uv`, `Vim`, and `Dagster`, and all three are correct, because the subject is
part of the sentence rather than a heading bolted to the front of it:
What does the --frozen option do when using uv run?
What is the difference between a temporary setting and a permanent setting in Vim?
Which tool is used to quickly scaffold a Python package containing a Dagster Definitions object?
What is wrong is `"uv: what does --frozen do?"` or `"Acme R&D: which committee approves Gate 4?"`.
The reviewer reads the context line, then reads it again. Drop the prefix, keep the sentence natural.
The line is read before the question, so it is part of the cue: it never holds an answer, and two
cards never differ by the line alone. How to pick its value is in `note-types.md`, "Choosing the
context value".
## Length
The Back is normally one sentence. Two when the second earns its place, as in the Vim card above
where the contrast is the fact. Past roughly 200 characters of prose, ask whether you are carding one
fact or several. Past 400, you almost certainly have a bundle: split it. Code is counted in lines
instead: one when it can be, up to six for lines that belong together, up to twelve for a task card
ending in a `Check:` line (see Code below).
The Front is normally under 100 characters. Longer is acceptable only when the extra words remove a
genuine ambiguity, or when the card presents a concrete case to reason about.
## Steps
The limit is the count: a Back holds at most three steps. Four or more is more than one card,
whether written as a list or as a sentence, and the linter counts list items for that reason.
Two steps are one sentence, joined with "then":
Back: Add the package to packages.yml, then run dbt deps.
Three steps are an `<ol>`. The numbers show the order and the count, so the reviewer knows how many
to recall and can check each one. Keep the items short and parallel, each opening with its verb.
Before, a real card:
Topic: Snowflake
Front: How do you rotate a key held in a user's RSA_PUBLIC_KEY property?

Back:

Pick the form by what the user will do with the code:
| The user will | Front | Back |
| Type it | The goal, with the names and values the code needs | The code: one line when it can be, up to six when the lines belong together |

| Write it for a task, a pattern, or an example | The task: the setting, the names, what the code must do, or "of your choice" | One solution, at most twelve lines, then a `Check:` line naming what every correct answer contains |
| Read it | A short snippet, asking what it returns, what it is for, or which line is wrong | The value, the purpose in one sentence, or the line and why |
| Recognise its key line | The snippet as a cloze Text, with the line that matters blanked | None, it is a cloze |
| Decide with it | Why it is built this way, what must hold, what breaks | One reason, in one sentence |

## Prose rules
Straight from the humanizer patterns, restricted to the ones that show up in card writing:
- No em dash. Use a comma, a period, or parentheses.
- No emoji anywhere. Source pages full of emoji headings get stripped, not mirrored.
- Straight quotes only, not curly.
- No bold for emphasis, and no bold-header bullet lists (`- **Thing:** explanation`).
- No significance inflation. Cut "plays a crucial role in", "is a key part of", "serves as".
Write "is". A card that says a thing is important is not testing anything.
- No "-ing" tails bolted onto a sentence: "..., highlighting the importance of governance".
- No rule-of-three padding. Three items only when there are exactly three.
- No hedging. "may possibly indicate" is not a recallable answer. If the source hedges, say who
hedges and how, or drop the card.
- No filler openers: "Note that", "It is important to note that", "Basically", "Essentially".
- Sentence case for anything heading-like.
## Source
Every card on the skill's note types says where its fact came from, so that the fact can be
checked, judged, and updated when the page changes (SuperMemo rule 18). The note type shows the
`Source` under the answer, in small type, and it is never part of what is recalled.
- A link to the exact page, with the page title as the link text. If the link dies, the title still
says what it was:
`Snowflake docs: Key-pair authentication`.
- Plain text when the source has no URL: a book and its chapter, a talk, or
`Conversation, 12 November 2026`. Never guess an address.
- Every card from one page carries the same `Source`. `"source:*docs.snowflake.com*"` finds every
card from that site, and `source:` with nothing after it finds the cards that have none.
- From a repository, link the file on its forge, under the repository's own address, as
`remembering-what-you-built` describes.
Volatility goes in the card text, not in the `Source`. Write "as of March 2026" in the Back or the
cloze sentence: the `Source` says where a fact came from, not how long it holds.
## Tags
Tags are for what no field and no note type says. The skill writes two, and taste decides neither.
`client::<name>`, such as `client::acme` or `client::globex`, goes on every card from client work.
Client cards go only to a model the client has cleared, and the repair queue's `--no-client` finds
them by this tag. The deck says the client only while the card sits in `Inbox::<project>`; the tag
keeps saying it once the card moves on. A personal project gets its deck and no tag. The client's
own document is still the `Source`.
`speed::fast` goes on every card that is quick to review by its shape, and on no other. A review
is reading the question, recalling, reading the answer and grading it, so a card is quick when there
is little to read and little to produce:
- each card's answer is at most 3 words and 30 characters: a Back, the text of one cloze index, or
the keys of a `Keyboard Shortcut` card, which always count as short;
- the question is at most 100 characters, and a cloze sentence at most 120 with its blanks filled;
- neither side holds a list, a code block, a table or an image.
A reversed note asks each side for the other, so both sides must be short. The linter applies the
rule to every draft, so a card asked to be tagged fast that the rule does not mark stays untagged,
and the response says why. A filtered deck searching `tag:speed::fast is:due` makes a queue of quick
reviews. Answer times would not do instead: a single card's are noisy (`principles.md`, "Tags").
Nothing else is a tag:
- The subject is the `Topic`.
- Where the fact came from is the `Source`.
- The kind of card is its note type: `note:"Keyboard Shortcut"` finds every shortcut.
- A card to fix gets marked during review, the `*` key, which the repair queue's `failing` check
picks up.
Anki writes `leech`, `marked`, `duplicate` and `db-check` itself. Never add one, and remove `leech`
only as part of a fix the user approved. Any other tag already in a collection is the user's: leave
it unless asked to clean up.

# The skill's note types
Every card this skill writes uses one of four note types. They are defined in
`assets/note-types.json`, each in the shape Anki's `createModel` takes, and share the styling in
`assets/card.css`.
| Note type | Fields | Use for |
| `Q&A by topic` | `Front`, `Topic`, `Back`, `Source` | Any question and answer: tools, concepts, domains, rules, science |
| `Cloze by topic` | `Text`, `Topic`, `Source` | Sentence-shaped facts, acronym pairs, closed lists, a code line blanked in context |

| `Keyboard Shortcut` | `Front`, `Topic`, `Shortcut`, `Shortcut (macOS)`, `Shortcut (Windows)`, `Shortcut (Linux)`, `Source` | Key bindings. `Shortcut` when the keys are the same everywhere, the per-OS fields when they differ |
| `Coding Exercises` | `Repository`, `Range` | A pointer to exercises worked in an editor, never a card about code |

with `Source`, shown under the answer: what goes in it is in `house-style.md`, "Source".
`Coding Exercises` is for a source that calls for writing a whole function or program, which is
practice rather than a card. Its one card reads "Finish exercises {{Range}} in the
{{Repository}} repository." Anki schedules the session, and the work happens in an
editor. Offer it instead of a long code Back, and only the user can name the repository: never
invent one.

`anki_cards.py check` reports each of the four as `ok`, `missing`, or `differs`:

approve, call `mcp__anki__createModel` with the arguments `anki_cards.py note-type "<name>"`

- **Differs.** The type exists but lacks a field, is the wrong kind, or does not show `{{Topic}}`

because it changes notes they already review. Renaming a field keeps every note, its templates
follow, and it needs no one-way sync. Adding, removing or reordering fields, and deleting a note

## Other note types in a collection
A collection usually holds more: Anki's stock `Basic` and `Cloze`, types added by an extension,
types built for one narrow workflow. Use none of them for a new card unless the user asks for that
type by name, and never hand-author notes for a type an extension writes. `Basic` has no context
field, so its Fronts lean on the deck to say what they are about and turn ambiguous once decks are
mixed or reorganised. For a fact that needs both directions, use one cloze note with `c1` and `c2`
rather than a reversed type. The linter warns on any type outside the four.

## Choosing the context value
`Topic` is free text, so consistency is on you. Reuse a value that already exists in the collection
instead of coining a near-duplicate. Check with:
```bash
python3 scripts/anki_cards.py topics --like "R&D"
The filter matches text, not meaning, so search under every name the subject goes by:
`--like JS` finds `Next.js` but not `JavaScript`.
Values are short noun phrases naming a tool or a subject, not sentences and not hierarchies, such as
`Causal Inference`, `Ableton Live`, `PEA`, `Snowflake`, `Server-sent events`, `Music Theory`.
The value is what the reviewer would already know at the moment they need the fact: the tool they
are working in, or the subject they are thinking about. Pick it at that level, never at the level of
the thing a card asks for:
- Never an answer. A value equal to a Back or a cloze deletion prints the answer above the question.
The usual case is a definition filed under a topic named after the thing it defines, as in
`{{c1::Fetch API}}` under the topic `Fetch API`, where `Web APIs` belongs. The linter rejects such
a note (worked example 12).
- Broad and shared. A value many cards share tells subjects apart; one that only a few cards carry
works as a hint.
- Never the tool when the card asks which tool to use. "Which tool both lints and formats Python,
replacing Flake8 and Black?" goes under `Python`, not `Ruff`.
- Never the only difference between two cards. "Give the Literal interface." under `hast` and again
under `mdast` is one question twice. The name that tells them apart goes in the question.
With broad decks and an `Inbox`, the deck does not say what a card is about. The `Topic` is the only
place a card's subject shows during review.
## Three API traps
1. `Cloze by topic` has no `Back Extra` field, only `Text`, `Topic` and `Source`. The MCP
`modelFieldNames` tool helpfully returns an `example` object mentioning `Back Extra` for anything
cloze-shaped, which is wrong here. Passing that key rejects the whole batch.
2. `mcp__anki__addNotes` takes one `deckName` and one `modelName` per call, capped at 100 notes.
A mixed set of Q&A and cloze cards therefore needs one call per model. Duplicates are skipped
individually, but a validation error such as an empty required field or a bad tag rejects the
entire batch, so lint before sending.
3. AnkiConnect drops a field the note type does not have, without an error. A `Source` sent to a
type made before the field existed is lost, which is why the linter checks field names against
the collection whenever Anki is up.
## Cloze conventions
Taken from real notes, verbatim:
{{c2::FR}} est l'acronyme de {{c1::Frais Réels}}.
A scope="module" fixture defined in {{c1::conftest.py}} is {{c1::shared by all test modules}} in that directory.
In the metric system, the prefix {{c1::deci-}} means {{c2::1/10}}.
Three patterns worth copying:
- Reuse the same index (`c1` twice) for blanks that must be recalled together on one card.
- Use `c1` and `c2` on the two halves of a pairing to get both directions from a single note. This is
the legitimate redundancy of SuperMemo rule 17, and it replaces a reversed note type.
- Blank the whole meaningful chunk, not one word out of a phrase. `{{c1::shared by all test modules}}`
rather than `shared by all {{c1::test modules}}`.
On index count: three is the ceiling when the blanks are separate facts sharing a sentence, because
past that the note is a bundle wearing a cloze costume. A genuine closed list, or a procedure laid
out as an `<ol>` with one index per step, is the exception, and one index per member is correct
there even at five or six. The linter warns above three either way, so justify the warning rather
than suppressing it.

## The five attributes
Matuschak's test for a prompt. Run a doubtful card against all five.
1. Focused. One detail. Too much detail in either the question or the answer produces a partial
retrieval, which is a partial memory.
2. Precise. The question specifies exactly what is being asked for. Vague questions produce vague
answers that do not reinforce anything in particular.
3. Consistent. The same answer every time. A prompt with several valid answers causes
retrieval-induced forgetting: recalling one answer actively inhibits the others.
4. Tractable. You should be right about ninety percent of the time. A card you keep failing is not
teaching you, it is churning.
5. Effortful. Retrieval, not inference. If the answer follows from the question by reasoning, you are
practising reasoning and not building the memory.
Consistent and effortful pull against each other, and that tension is where most bad cards live. Add
enough context to force one answer, but not so much that the question's shape becomes the cue.
## Minimum information principle (SuperMemo 4)
Formulate the smallest piece of knowledge that stands on its own. Simple items get scheduled well by
the algorithm because performance on them is stable. Complex items produce partial recall, which the
scheduler cannot interpret, so they need redundant repetition at awkward intervals.
The canonical example is a "characteristics of the Dead Sea" card carrying location, depth, length,
salinity, and density at once. It becomes five cards, each of which the scheduler can then handle
independently, dropping the easy ones fast and drilling the hard one.
Practical consequence: cards are cheap. Matuschak puts the lifetime cost of a prompt at ten to thirty
seconds of review across its first year. Splitting one bad card into three good ones is close to free.
Write more cards than feels necessary, but only about material you actually care about.
## Sets, enumerations, and closed lists (SuperMemo 9 and 10)
Three distinct cases, three different treatments.
A set is an unordered group: "which countries are in the EU". Never card it directly. Listing members
in a different order each review has, in Wozniak's words, a disastrous effect on memory. Convert to
individual membership facts, or to the historical sequence that produced the set, or drop it.
An enumeration is ordered: steps in a process, a pipeline, a gate sequence. Better than a set because
the order forces a consistent traversal, but still hard. Wozniak's fix is overlapping cloze
deletions, so each card asks for one step in context rather than the whole chain. Anki's stock cloze
is the weaker form: each card blanks one step and shows all the others, later ones included. Hiding
the later steps would need a cloned Cloze note type styled through Anki's `.cloze-inactive` class,
and the skill's note types include none, so do not promise that behaviour. Procedures get their own
section below.
A closed list has a fixed, small, known membership: the five R&D pillars, the four criteria for
selecting a country. Write one cloze card per member on a single note, so each member is retrieved
separately with the others visible as context. That is the one case where a multi-index cloze note is
the right answer.
An open list has no fixed membership: "examples of a design pattern", "functions this library
exposes". Do not write a fill-in-the-blank card. Instead write cards linking each instance to the
category, cards about the pattern the instances share, and a generative card asking for any example.
## Procedures
A procedure is an enumeration with a purpose, and the purpose decides what to card. Matuschak works
through a recipe in the prompts essay. A cloze per step over the full step list is "an awfully
unfocused prompt", so he cuts the procedure down instead:
1. Drop the steps anyone doing the task would infer. Of the recipe's four steps, "the first and
fourth steps aren't worth writing prompts about."
2. Card the keywords: the verb, adverb, or quantity that is easy to get wrong.
3. Card the transitions: "conditions or heuristics describing when to move between verbs are
important." In a key rotation, that is when the old key may be removed.
4. Card the why: "Explanation-type prompts are especially valuable when studying procedures."
5. Optionally, one card for the whole sequence. Wozniak grades a whole sequence next to the items
that cover its parts (the EU example under rule 9), and lets poems stay whole "due to strong
semantic connections" until you stumble, then splits them with cloze. Do the same: three steps
at most, each leading to the next, and split the card when it starts to lapse.
When the outline itself must be known, Matuschak's list form is simpler: a numbered cloze, one index
per step, each step cut to its keywords, in a fixed order. "When each element has a consistent
(though arbitrary) location, you'll end up learning the list's visual 'shape'."
All of this is practitioner experience, and no controlled study compares procedure cards. Cognitive
science agrees with it indirectly. Story events on a causal chain are recalled better than dead ends
(Trabasso and van den Broek, 1985). Ordered recall degrades as a sequence grows, mostly by swapping
neighbouring items (Hurlstone, Hitch and Baddeley, 2014). Learners grading their own multi-part
answers often credit partial or wrong recall (Dunlosky and colleagues, 2011).
### Lists and sentences on the Back
No study compares list and sentence answers on flashcards. The sources agree on the count rather
than the markup: Wozniak treats every enumeration as hard, and
[Woehlke](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7Q7DPSk4iGFJd8DRk/an-opinionated-guide-to-using-anki-correctly)
puts the ceiling at "3 logical bullets". On format, they split by count:
- Two items read better as one line. Nielsen Norman Group: shorter lists "work better embedded in a
sentence". Woehlke finds a two-bullet card "quicker to recall as one long bullet". The connective
carries the order, as pointer words carried structure in Mautone and Mayer (2001).
- From three items, a numbered list. Nielsen Norman Group numbers a list when "the order or the
final count" matters. Wozniak numbers his own sequence answer, "(1) France and (2) Germany, Italy
and the Benelux", and in [knowledge structuring](https://super-memory.com/english/ol/ks.htm) finds
that when enumerated items keep their order, "their spatial location will strongly be imprinted".
Matuschak keeps lists in a fixed order so the reviewer learns their visual "shape". In Jansen
(2014), bulleted lists improved recall of the items in three of five studies. Separate items also
make it easy to check an answer one idea at a time, which cuts overconfident self-grading
(Dunlosky and colleagues, 2011).
- A long-time user of these cards finds that the visible count helps recall.
The size problem is the count, not the markup. In one collection read on 2026-10-25, 107 of the 291
Q&A Backs written as HTML lists held four or more items. The linter counts list items, so a long
list is flagged like a long sentence.
## Code and source code
No study compares code-writing cards with prose concept cards for working programmers. The rules in
`SKILL.md` combine four kinds of evidence, and every one of them is indirect.
You get better at the retrieval you practise. Across 122 experiments, transfer from testing was
strongest when the practice and the test shared the response (Pan and Rickard, 2018). Fact quizzes
did not improve higher-order test questions, higher-order quizzes did not improve fact questions,
and a mix did well on both (Agarwal, 2019, with college and middle-school students and prose
passages). A card that asks for the call trains typing the call; a card that asks why trains the
why. Neither substitutes for the other.
No order wins. Conceptual and procedural knowledge build each other in both directions, and no study
compares concepts first with procedures first. The one classroom ordering experiment found that
alternating lessons taught procedures better than a block of concepts first, with concepts learned
about equally (Rittle-Johnson, Schneider and Star, 2015; Rittle-Johnson and Koedinger, 2009, with
schoolchildren). Practitioners agree on one order only: understand the code and run it, then card it
(Wozniak, rules 1 and 2; Kinsella; Nielsen).
Short answers. Producing an answer beats studying it for material with few interacting parts, and
the advantage shrinks or reverses as the parts multiply, unless the learner is already expert
(Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller, 2015; van Gog and Sweller, 2015). Karpicke and Aue (2015) dispute the
reversal, but their own reanalysis supports only a small benefit. Long answers are also graded
leniently: middle-school students credited 73 percent of their wrong definitions with no standard
and 44 percent with the correct one in view (Lipko and colleagues, 2009), and in college students
lenient grading went with worse retention (Dunlosky and Rawson, 2012). Experts do not store code
verbatim. They recall a real program far better than shuffled code, and organise code by what it
does rather than by syntax (Shneiderman, 1976; Adelson, 1981; Soloway and Ehrlich, 1984).
Completion and prediction fit a card. Novices who completed programs built programs better than
those who wrote them from scratch (van Merriënboer, 1990), Parsons problems took less time than
writing for the same learning (Ericson, Margulieux and Rick, 2017), and novices who predicted what
code prints learned more than those taught by tell-and-practice (Tucker and colleagues, 2024,
d = 0.36). A code cloze and a "what does this return" card are their card-sized forms. A prediction
card repeated verbatim turns into recall of one answer, so write variants when the rule is the point
(Matuschak).
Patterns are worth keeping whole. Experts hold programming plans, generic fragments for stereotyped
goals, and the rules for combining them (Soloway and Ehrlich, 1984), so the pattern, not one
particular program, is what is worth keeping. Rearranging and completing the lines of a pattern
taught it better than writing or tracing code, and improved code writing in general as much as
writing practice did (Weinman, Fox and Hearst, 2021, with 237 students). Producing an answer also
overtakes studying for complex material once the learner knows the domain (Chen, Kalyuga and
Sweller, 2015, Experiment 2), which describes a working programmer meeting a pattern in a language
they already write. A larger card is still harder to grade, which is why a task card carries a
`Check:` line: grading against listed parts cut overconfidence further than seeing the whole answer
(Lipko and colleagues, 2009). Nielsen keeps a larger question as an integrative card on top of its
atomic pieces. Knowing when a pattern applies is a separate skill, trained by a card that gives the
situation and asks which pattern fits: mixing problem types in practice beat blocking them by type
a week later (Rohrer and Taylor, 2007, with college students), and a review queue already mixes
topics.
Examples and tasks are the most direct practice for writing code, and what counts against them is
grading, not asking. Producing a new example is one of the generative prompts listed under "Prompt
types beyond bare recall", judged on whether it is right rather than on whether it matches.
Execute Program checks every answer by running it in an interpreter, so two different correct
programs both pass (Matuschak's notes on it), and its larger prompts give a listing and a goal to
reach, which is a task card graded by a machine. An application prompt repeated in the same words
turns into recall of one answer, which a new example each time, or a second situation, avoids
(Matuschak). Recalling a command when asked for it is not recognising the moment to use it in the
command line (Nielsen), which is why a task describes the situation rather than naming the tool.
What goes wrong is the grade: with one long reference to compare against, a learner credits near
misses (Lipko and colleagues, 2009), so a task card names the parts it is graded on in a `Check:`
line, and the user runs the answer when only running it would tell.
Whole programs are practice. Spaced repetition keeps a skill and practice raises it (Gwern).
Matuschak sketches a separate expanding queue of exercises for skills, and Skerritt schedules whole
LeetCode problems through Anki as pointers, solved outside it each time they fall due.
A codebase. The code stays there to re-read, and it changes by the thousand elements a day (Fritz
and colleagues, 2010). Developers recall its method-level detail worse than its architecture and
intent, and say that detail is not worth remembering (Krüger and Hebig, 2020). What they find
hardest to recover is what the code does not say: 66 percent rated understanding the rationale
behind code a serious problem (LaToza, Venolia and DeLine, 2006, with Microsoft engineers),
rationale and intent were the most frequent hard-to-answer questions (LaToza and Myers, 2010), and
why code was written a particular way was among the searches most often deferred (Ko, DeLine and
Venolia, 2007). Nielsen cards an API while a project uses it and deletes the cards after, Kinsella
came to regret his cards on third-party library APIs, and Wozniak cards a call only when reviewing
it costs less than looking it up.
One collection's computer-science decks, read 2026-11-12. Within the same context value, one-line
code answers had a lower Again rate than prose answers in 16 of 20 shared values (median 17 against
27 percent) and took a median 7 seconds against 11. At intervals of three weeks or more, one-line
code answers passed 77 percent of reviews (n = 176) and prose answers over 60 characters 23 percent
(n = 61). Multi-line code passed 56 to 66 percent at every length, with no drop from two or three
lines to four to six, but its cost climbed with length: a median 14, 18, 31 and 47 seconds per
answer at two to three, four to six, seven to ten, and eleven or more lines, with 12, 16, 29 and 42
percent of answers at Anki's 60-second cap. Scenario cards, which give code or a table and ask for
the code that uses it, did best among the long ones (12 percent Again, 83 percent passed after three
weeks, n = 18) at 46 seconds a review. Open "write an example" cards of four lines or more did
worse: 21 percent Again and 60 percent passed after three weeks (n = 10), at 41 seconds. Both groups
are small. This is observational: what gets written as one line is probably also easier, and long
answers are graded leniently.
## Interference (SuperMemo 11)
Wozniak calls interference probably the single greatest cause of forgetting in a mature collection.
It is the failure mode of carding a source that presents many parallel items, which is exactly what
an org chart, an acronym glossary, or an API surface looks like.
Symptoms: you recall that there are six committees but cannot attach the right mandate to the right
acronym, and each review reinforces the confusion.
Countermeasures, in order of preference:
1. Card fewer of them. Six near-identical facts you half-remember are worth less than two you know.
2. Differentiate by content. Ask for the distinguishing property, not the label. "Which committee
makes major investment decisions" separates cleanly from "which committee evaluates benefit and
risk", where "what does PIC stand for" and "what does BRC stand for" do not.
3. Add a personal or concrete hook (rules 14 and 15), such as the one decision you actually saw a
committee make.
4. Space the introduction. Card two today and two next week rather than six at once.
## Optimize wording (SuperMemo 12) and context cues (SuperMemo 16)
Every word in a card is read on every review, so redundant words have a recurring cost and no
benefit. The SuperMemo example compresses "What does GRE stand for in biochemistry?" to
`bioch: GRE`, moving the domain out of the question and into a context label.
The skill's note types implement that label as the `Topic` field. Using it is not optional
politeness, it is the mechanism that lets Fronts stay short without becoming ambiguous: in one
collection read on 2026-11-12, 70 percent of the Q&A Fronts did not contain their own context value.
Every practitioner and tool surveyed shows such a cue before the question. Wozniak's label "puts
your brain immediately in the right context", Bjornstad wants the topic "stated at the beginning or
near the beginning of the question", and Orbit, Obsidian Spaced Repetition, RemNote, Logseq and
Mnemosyne all show one by default. Nielsen, merging his decks into one, had to rewrite "How to delete
a word?" as "In Emacs, how to delete a word?". None of them treats a tool differently from any other
subject. That collection did, with a `Tool` field and note types of its own, and the split never
held: seven of its ten largest topics were software, and 18 values appeared in both fields.
### What the line may say
No study tests a topic line on flashcards, so what follows is extrapolated, but it points one way.
A cue shared by many items does little to bring back any one of them (Watkins and Watkins, 1975),
and how well a cue singles out its target predicts recall better than how closely it matches the
study context (Goh and Lu, 2012). The line's job is to rule out other readings of the question, not
to help recall. Practice retrieval with fewer cues left better memories (Carpenter and DeLosh, 2006),
so a line that narrows the answer costs retention. Matuschak asks for "enough context that
reasonable alternative answers are clearly wrong, while not including so much context that you
encourage pattern matching", and RemNote's help warns that its context display "can result in giving
the answer away".
Two consequences. Similar facts interfere less when their cues differ (Diaz and Benjamin, 2011), so
the question, not the line, must tell siblings apart. And a label that announces the category means
the learner never practises choosing it (Rohrer, Dedrick and Stershic, 2015), so a card asking which
tool to use must not name the tool above the question.
The same collection, read 2026-11-12: 45 notes had a Back or a cloze deletion equal to their own
context value, 44 of them clozes and 29 in one deck of Web API definitions. Values used by one to
three notes leaked on 14.7 percent of their notes, values used by more than twenty on 0.2 percent.
## Legitimate redundancy (SuperMemo 17)
Redundancy does not contradict the minimum information principle when it encodes the same fact from a
genuinely different angle:
- Both directions of a pairing. Term to definition and definition to term. Use `c1` and `c2` on one
cloze note.
- An explanation card alongside a fact card. What it is, and why it is that way.
- Intermediate steps of a derivation as their own cards.
- The same concept in a different representation, for example a formula and a graph.
Two cards asking the same question in slightly different words is not redundancy, it is waste, and it
creates the inconsistency problem from attribute 3.
## Prompt types beyond bare recall
Recall cards are the floor, not the ceiling. When the material is conceptual rather than factual,
reach for:
- Explanation. Why does this hold, how does the mechanism work.
- Application. Given this situation, what does this concept tell you to do.
- Connection. How does this relate to, differ from, or generalise something already known.
- Creative or generative. Produce a new example. The answer varies, so accept anything valid. Judge
these against attribute 4 rather than 3.
- Salience. Keep an idea available at the moment it is relevant, by tying it to a decision you make.
## How much to card
Start at five to ten cards per article or chapter. Completionism is the failure mode: it drains the
motivation that the whole system depends on, and produces cards about material you do not care about,
which you will then fail and resent.
It is hard to write good cards on first exposure to unfamiliar material. For a difficult source, card
the basic factual scaffolding first, and write the conceptual cards on a second pass once you
understand it.
Delete cards you no longer care about. A card that survives only out of sunk cost is a tax.
## Sources and date stamps (SuperMemo 18 and 19)
Record where a fact came from, so you can verify it, judge its reliability, and update it when it
changes. Stamp anything volatile with a date or version: statistics with the year collected, software
behaviour with the version, org structures and prices with the date read.
Each of those uses means reopening the page, so the source is a link to it, in the `Source` field,
and the date goes in the visible card text. Wozniak's placement fits: sources "should accompany your
items but should not be part of the learned knowledge", so the link sits under the answer and never
on the question. Bjornstad starts with a tag for a whole book and adds a field only once he wants
the exact page, because fussing over precision can make adding cards painful. An agent writes the
field, so the exact page costs nothing. One collection read on 2026-11-12 kept its sources as tags:
`aws-docs` sat on 44 notes, and none of its 544 source-tagged notes recorded which page a fact came
from.
## Tags
Anki's manual gives tags one piece of advice: think "in advance about how you want to use them". A
tag belongs to the note, so every card of the note shares it. Research on personal information adds
two cautions. People rarely find things again by tag: in Whittaker and colleagues' field study of
email, tags were 1 percent of the ways people reached a message again, search 18 percent. And
vocabularies coined as you go drift into synonyms and mismatched levels of detail (Golder and
Huberman), while one short list per independent question holds up (Hearst). So a tag here answers
one of two questions no field or note type answers, each decided by a rule: which client a card
belongs to, which decides who may read it, and whether the card is quick to review.
The same collection held 207 distinct tags on 757 of its 8,966 notes, 87 of them used once, with
pairs such as `fingerprint` and `fingerprinting`.
Quick to review is a property of the card's shape, worked out by a rule rather than measured. Anki
times a review from the question to the grade, so one card's times are noisy: in that collection,
read 2026-11-15, 8.9 percent of the recorded reviews sat at the 60-second cap, a card left open, and
reviews done on the move run slow. Over many cards the noise averages out, and there the rule in
`house-style.md` separates the cards: those it marks took a median 5.0 seconds a review, three
quarters of them 7.0 or less, against 11.9 seconds for the rest, three quarters of them 7.9 or more
(1,008 and 4,127 cards with three or more reviews). Nothing is reviewed in under a second by that
clock: 2 of the 5,135 cards had a median that low. Speed also comes from practice (Logan), so a card
gets quicker as it is learnt; the rule marks the cards that stay cheap even when they are failed,
because a short answer is quick to check. How easy a card is to memorise is another property, which
FSRS works out for each card from its grades alone: `prop:d<0.3` finds the easy ones, with no tag.
## Leaving the Inbox
A note leaves its project deck once every card has an interval of 21 days or more, the line Anki
itself draws between young and mature cards. The interval comes from the grades through the
scheduler, not from answer times, so a distracted review does not move it. A card at three weeks
has been recalled across a gap long enough to show the memory holds. From there it joins a broad
deck, mixed in with other subjects, which is what the manual recommends: "Lots of little decks may
mean you end up seeing cards in a recognizable order", and that "leads to weaker memories". On
2026-11-15, no studied Inbox card in that collection had an interval past a week.
# The repair queue
Reviews show which cards fail, which are slow to answer, and, through the `Source`, which have gone
out of date. Reading a card cold shows none of that: in the [Memory Machines
study](https://memory-machines.com/report) (Kirkby and Matuschak, 2026), no model judging prompts it
had never reviewed passed 70% at telling usable ones from broken ones, and the flaws it missed most
were wordiness and questions with several right answers. So the checks pick cards from the review
history, in code, and your part is the judgement: why this card, what to change, or nothing.
A check never changes the collection. It adds proposals to a queue, and the user approves them later
through the same approval table as every other change.
## The checks
`anki_cards.py candidates <kind>` prints the candidates as JSON: each note's fields, tags, cards,
lapses and reviews, and the `signal` that picked it.
| Kind | Picks | Why it is worth a look |

| `failing` | Notes marked for repair; cards first answered in the last 60 days and failed 3 or more times since; cards with 2 or more lapses. Each failed in the last `--days`, 7 by default | The plainest evidence that a card is broken, and a new card costs the least to fix |

| `slow` | Cards in the slowest tenth by median answer time in review, over 3 or more answers in the last 90 days, or at `--seconds` and slower | A card passed slowly is usually wordy, vague, or a list in disguise, the flaws models judge worst |
| `sourced` | Notes with a `Source`, at random | A wrong or outdated fact passes every review. The source gives the check something to compare with |
| `random` | Notes studied in the last 90 days, at random | A control. When it finds little the other checks missed, stop running it |

| `inbox` | Notes in the Inbox and its project decks with a lint error. Beside them, under `proposals`: each learnt Inbox note's move, and every note in the collection whose `speed::fast` tag disagrees with its rule | New cards get a second look while they are still being learnt, and two rules move notes on and keep the tag true without anyone deciding |
Marking is how the user asks for a repair while reviewing: Mark Note, the `*` key, puts Anki's
`marked` tag on the note, and the next `failing` run picks it up whether or not the card failed.
The queue holds a note back while a proposal for it is pending, for a cool-down after a check of the
same kind closed one (30 days for `failing`, 90 for `slow`, `random` and `inbox`, 180 for
`sourced`), and for 30 days after any fix was applied, so that the fix has reviews to show for
itself. A marked note waits only while a proposal is pending: marking it again is a new request.
The inbox check rests its moves, its tag changes and its diagnoses apart, so a kept diagnosis never
holds back a move, and a move or a tag change, which fixes nothing, holds a note back from no check.
`--max` caps the candidates, worst first for `failing` and `slow`; the inbox check's proposals are
never capped. `--no-client` leaves out notes tagged `client::<name>`, for a run on a model the
client has not cleared.
## Diagnosis and action
Run the self-audit in SKILL.md on each candidate, read its signal, and give it one diagnosis and one
action. The signal says where to look, not what is wrong: a card fails because it asks for two
things, because the fact is hard, or because the user never learnt what it builds on.
| Diagnosis | Action | The proposal carries |
| Fine as it is: the signal has another cause, such as a code task that is long by design | `keep` | the reason, in `diagnosis` |
| Badly formed: a set, two questions, several defensible answers, a vague Front | `rewrite`, or `split` when it holds two facts | `fields`, or `newNotes`; a split deletes the old note |
| Missing prerequisite: it cannot be answered without something the collection does not hold | `prerequisite` | `newNotes` for the missing facts, filed to `Inbox`, or a `resource` to read first |
| Confused with a sibling, found with `mcp__anki__findNotes` on the same `Topic` | `differentiate` | `fields` that put the name telling them apart in the question |
| Wrong or out of date against its `Source` | `fix-fact` | `fields`, with the date or version in the text |
| Not worth its reviews: it fails the sigh test, or nothing the user does needs it | `suspend` or `delete` | the reason, in `diagnosis` |
Every proposal follows SKILL.md: house style, and no fact its source does not state. Keep the
`Source` the note has. When it has none, say so in the diagnosis rather than guess one, as in the
Inbox; only a prerequisite card, a new fact, names the page it comes from. Before writing a
prerequisite card, search the collection for the fact under every name it goes by. A rewrite that
keeps the fact keeps the card's history; a split, a delete and a change of note type lose it, so the
diagnosis says so.
Before drafting, read the verdicts already given on the subject:
`anki_cards.py queue list --status decided --topic "<Topic>"`. A rejection's reason is the user's
taste, stated once. Follow it rather than proposing the same change again.
## Proposals
`anki_cards.py queue add <file>` takes one proposal or a JSON array of them. It checks each against
its note as it stands and refuses a batch in which any proposal brings a lint error the note did not
already have, appending nothing until the whole batch passes. An old gap, such as a `Source` nobody
can name any more, does not block a fix; it shows in the approval table instead.
```json
{"kind": "failing", "noteId": 1794100000001, "action": "rewrite", "model": "<the model drafting>",
"signal": "lapsed 4 times, last failed on 2026-11-12",
"diagnosis": "\"What about autovacuum?\" fits several answers. Ask for the one the Back gives.",
"fields": {"Front": "When does autovacuum process a table?"}},
{"kind": "slow", "noteId": 1794100000002, "action": "keep",
"diagnosis": "A nine-line task card ending in a Check: line, slow by design and never failed."}
`fields` holds only the fields that change. Each of `newNotes` has the shape of a draft,
`{"deckName", "modelName", "fields", "tags"}`, and never names an archived deck. A field fix needs no
`tags`: when its new fields change what the `speed::fast` rule says, `queue add` records the tag
change beside it, to apply with the fields.
## The inbox check
Its `proposals` come from rules and carry their own diagnosis: queue the array exactly as printed.
Each is one of two actions:
| Action | Decided by | The proposal carries |

| `move` | Every card of the note has an interval of 21 days or more. It goes to the current deck holding the most cards with its `Topic` | `toDeck`, or null when no current deck holds the Topic and the user names one |
| `retag` | The `speed::fast` rule in `house-style.md` disagrees with the note's tag | `tags`, `{"add": ["speed::fast"]}` or `{"remove": ["speed::fast"]}` |
`queue add` refuses a move for a note that is not learnt, a move to an archive or into the Inbox, a
tag change the rule does not call for, and either action from any other check. The check's
`candidates` are notes in the Inbox with a lint error, which get a diagnosis and an action like any
check's. A note gets one proposal a run, a diagnosis first, then a tag change, then a move: the
others wait for the next run.
## Running unattended
A scheduled run has nobody to approve, so it calls no Anki tool that writes: no `addNotes`,
`updateNoteFields`, `deleteNotes`, `changeDeck`, `addTags`, `removeTags`, suspension or
`createModel`. It asks no questions either.
1. Run `anki_cards.py candidates <kind>` with the flags the schedule names. When AnkiConnect is
unreachable, run `anki_cards.py queue skip --kind <kind> --reason "AnkiConnect unreachable"` and
stop: the report counts missed runs, so silence never reads as a clean week.
2. Work through the candidates in order. After every few, write their proposals to a file and run
`queue add`, so that a run cut short keeps what it finished. Fix a refused batch and add it again.
The inbox check's `proposals` go to `queue add` first, as printed.
3. Queue a `keep` for every candidate that needs nothing. It counts in the report and holds the note
back from the next runs.
4. End with one line: the candidates, and how many of each action.
## Going through the queue
When the user asks to go through their repair queue:
1. Run `anki_cards.py queue list`. It names any report saved since the last verdict; show that
first.
2. Read the proposals from `queue list --json` and show them as the approval table: the card as it
stands, the proposal, the diagnosis, and what the change costs in review history.
3. Apply what the user approves as "Reviewing existing cards" in SKILL.md says, then record each
verdict: `anki_cards.py queue decide <id>... --status applied`, or `--status rejected --reason
"<their reason>"`. A rejection needs the reason, in the user's words, because later runs read it.
A rule's proposals go in the table grouped, the moves by destination and the tag changes as one
row. A `move` goes through `mcp__anki__changeDeck`, with every card of the note read fresh from
`notesInfo`, to its `toDeck`. When `toDeck` is null, ask for a deck, a broad category the user
studies on its own, or reject the move with their words when they keep the note with its
project. A proposal's `tags`, on a `retag` or beside a field fix, goes through
`mcp__anki__addTags` or `mcp__anki__removeTags`.
4. Remove the `marked` tag from the notes `queue decide` names, with `mcp__anki__removeTags`.
## The report
`anki_cards.py queue report` tabulates, for each check over the last 30 days, the notes checked, the
share that needed a change, the share of proposals the user accepted, the pending ones, and the runs
that could not reach Anki. For field fixes applied at least 30 days ago, it compares Again presses
per answer in the 30 days before the proposal with the 30 days after the fix. `--save` also writes
it to `reports/` beside the queue file.
Read it for what to change, not as a score. A check whose proposals are mostly rejected costs the
user time: pause it. A fix that keeps coming back, the same flaw in card after card, belongs in this
skill as a rule or a worked example, where it stops the next cards from being written that way.
## The queue file
`anki-flashcards/queue.jsonl` in the XDG state directory, `~/.local/state` unless `$XDG_STATE_HOME`
says otherwise; `--queue` points elsewhere. It holds card text, so it stays out of every repository.
One JSON record per line, appended and never rewritten:
- `proposal`: `id`, `at`, `kind`, `noteId`, `cardIds`, `topic`, `action`, `diagnosis`, `signal`,
`fields`, `newNotes`, `resource`, `toDeck`, `tags`, `model`
- `decision`: `id`, `at`, `status` (`applied` or `rejected`), `reason`
- `skip`: `at`, `kind`, `reason`
## On a schedule
Each check runs as a schedule of its own, which starts a fresh agent in a project that installs this
skill and the anki MCP server. With Paseo, unattended in oh-my-pi's full mode:
```sh
paseo schedule create --name anki-failing --cron "0 20 * * *" --timezone <zone> \
--provider omp/<model> --mode full --thinking medium --cwd <project> \

"Run the failing check of the anki-flashcards repair queue unattended, as its references/repair-queue.md says: python3 .agents/skills/anki-flashcards/scripts/anki_cards.py candidates failing --max 20"
- Run `failing` daily, `inbox` weekly, the other checks weekly or monthly, and `queue report --save`
monthly.
- Archive on finish can stay on: everything a run produces is in the queue.
- Anki must be open when a run fires. On macOS, App Nap must be off for Anki, or AnkiConnect stops
answering in the background: `defaults write net.ankiweb.dtop NSAppSleepDisabled -bool true`, then
restart Anki.
- Client cards go only to a model the client has cleared, so give the other runs `--no-client`. The
inbox check moves client cards too, so it runs on a cleared model, without the flag.

Every "before" below started as a real card. Most came from a client's Confluence page on its R&D
structure and were deleted for being bad. The client is called Acme here, and its committees and
figures are renamed. Read these to calibrate how short a good Back is and how much gets cut.
## 1. Two facts in one card
The single most common failure. A Front with "and" in it is two cards.
Before, note type `Basic`:

Back: Portfolio Investment Council — major investment decisions.

## 7. Bundled comparison that is genuinely one card
Not everything long is wrong. This real card stays as it is:
Topic: Vim
Front: What is the difference between a temporary setting and a permanent setting in Vim?
Back: A temporary setting (e.g., :set number) is lost when Vim closes. A permanent setting is written to vimrc and persists across sessions.

## 8. Volatile fact needing a date stamp
The source page was generated by an AI tool and last modified in March 2026, and it describes an org
structure. Both facts belong in the card:

Front: How many functional pillars was R&D organised around as of March 2026?
Back:  Five, each with its own Function Head.
Source: R&D governance
Without "as of March 2026" this card silently becomes wrong after the next reorganisation, and there

## 9. A procedure as the only card
A real card:
Q&A by topic
Topic: Snowflake
Front: How do you rotate a key held in a user's RSA_PUBLIC_KEY property?

Back:
  1. Set the new key in RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2
  2. Switch clients to the new private key
  3. UNSET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY
Three ordered steps, each needed before the next, so one card for the whole sequence is defensible
and the `<ol>` is the right form. Two small fixes: the third item is a bare command among
instructions, and "new key" does not say which of the two new keys goes in the property. The bigger
problem is that this is the only card, so the step that can lock clients out, unsetting the old key,
is tested only as a position in a sequence.
After, two notes:
Q&A by topic
Topic: Snowflake
Front: How do you rotate a key held in a user's RSA_PUBLIC_KEY property?

Back:
  1. Set the new public key in RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2
  2. Switch clients to the new private key
  3. Run UNSET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY
Source: Snowflake docs: Key-pair authentication
Q&A by topic
Topic: Snowflake
Front: During a key rotation, when can you UNSET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY?
Back:  After clients have switched to the new private key.
Source: Snowflake docs: Key-pair authentication
The first is a field update, so it keeps its review history. The second is a new note, and the one
to keep if you keep only one: it asks for the transition, which is where the procedure goes wrong.

"""Each proposal with its status, pending, kept, applied or rejected, and when it closed."""
verdicts = {record["id"]: record for record in records if record.get("type") == "decision"}
states = []
for record in records:
if record.get("type") != "proposal":
continue
state = dict(record, status="pending", closedAt=None)
verdict = verdicts.get(record["id"])
if record.get("action") == "keep":
state.update(status="kept", closedAt=record["at"])

def held_back(states: list[dict], kind: str, now: datetime.datetime, group: str | None = None) -> tuple[set, set]:

applied within SETTLE_DAYS, which needs reviews before anyone can tell whether it worked. With a
group, only proposals in that group of actions count, so a kept diagnosis never holds back a
move, and a move or a retag, which fixes nothing, never holds back a check."""
pending, resting = set(), set()
for state in states:
if state["status"] == "pending":
pending.add(state["noteId"])

mine = state["kind"] == kind and (group is None or action_group(state.get("action")) == group)
settling = (group in (None, "fix") and state["status"] == "applied"
and state.get("action") not in RULE_ACTIONS and age < SETTLE_DAYS)

def check_field_change(where: str, note: dict, fields, errors: list, warnings: list) -> dict | None:
"""A field change may not bring a lint error the note did not have. Old gaps, such as a Source
nobody can name any more, are the user's to see, not a reason to refuse the fix. Returns the
speed::fast change the new fields call for, which is applied with them."""
if not isinstance(fields, dict) or not fields:
errors.append("%s: give the new field values in fields." % where)
return None
before = ordered_fields(note)
unknown = [name for name in fields if name not in before]
if unknown:
errors.append("%s: %s not a field of %r." % (where, ", ".join(map(repr, unknown)), note["modelName"]))
return None
after = dict(before)
after.update(fields)
if after == before:
errors.append("%s: the fields are unchanged." % where)
return None
after_tags, change = speed_tags(note["modelName"], after, note["tags"])
old_errors, old_warnings = lint_findings(note["modelName"], list(before), before, note["tags"])
new_errors, new_warnings = lint_findings(note["modelName"], list(before), after, after_tags)
errors += ["%s: %s" % (where, message) for message in sorted(new_errors - old_errors)]
warnings += ["%s: %s" % (where, message) for message in sorted(new_warnings - old_warnings)]
return change
def check_move(where: str, note: dict, to_deck, errors: list) -> None:
"""A move takes a learnt note out of the Inbox: to a current deck, or to none yet, when the user
names one at approval."""
if to_deck is not None and (not isinstance(to_deck, str) or not to_deck.strip()):
errors.append("%s: toDeck is a deck name, or null for the user to name one." % where)
return
if to_deck and (to_deck.startswith(ARCHIVE_PREFIX) or to_deck == INBOX_DECK or to_deck.startswith(INBOX_DECK + "::")):
errors.append("%s: %s is an archive or the Inbox, where a learnt note never goes." % (where, to_deck))
if not learnt(cards_info(note.get("cards") or [])):
errors.append("%s: not learnt yet, a card's interval is under %d days." % (where, LEARNT_DAYS))
def check_retag(where: str, note: dict, tags, errors: list) -> None:
"""A retag makes speed::fast follow its rule, and changes nothing else."""
fields = ordered_fields(note)
change = speed_tags(note["modelName"], fields, note["tags"])[1]
if not change:
errors.append("%s: %s already follows its rule on this note." % (where, FAST_TAG))
elif tags != change:
errors.append("%s: the rule's tag change is %s, not %s." % (where, json.dumps(change), json.dumps(tags)))
def check_new_notes(where: str, note: dict, action: str, proposal: dict, errors: list, warnings: list) -> None:
"""New notes are linted as drafts. A split may carry its note's old gaps, such as a missing
Source; a prerequisite is a new fact and needs everything a new card needs."""
new_notes = proposal.get("newNotes")
resource = proposal.get("resource")
if action == "prerequisite" and not new_notes and isinstance(resource, str) and resource.strip():
return
if not isinstance(new_notes, list) or not new_notes:
errors.append("%s: a %s needs newNotes%s." % (where, action, ", or a resource to read" if action == "prerequisite" else ""))
return
inherited: set = set()
if action == "split":
current = ordered_fields(note)
inherited, _ = lint_findings(note["modelName"], list(current), current, speed_tags(note["modelName"], current, [])[0])
for number, new in enumerate(new_notes, 1):
label = "%s, new note %d" % (where, number)
if not isinstance(new, dict) or not new.get("deckName") or not new.get("modelName"):
errors.append("%s: needs deckName, modelName and fields." % label)
continue
if new["deckName"].startswith(ARCHIVE_PREFIX):
errors.append("%s: %s is archived. New notes go to %s or a current deck." % (label, new["deckName"], INBOX_DECK))
try:
names = field_names(new["modelName"])
except RuntimeError:
errors.append("%s: the note type %r does not exist." % (label, new["modelName"]))
continue
new_errors, new_warnings = lint_findings(new["modelName"], list(names), new.get("fields") or {}, new.get("tags") or [])
errors += ["%s: %s" % (label, message) for message in sorted(new_errors - inherited)]
warnings += ["%s: %s" % (label, message) for message in sorted(new_warnings)]

def share(part: int, whole: int) -> str:
return "%d of %d (%d%%)" % (part, whole, round(100 * part / whole)) if whole else "-"
def fix_effects(states: list[dict], now: datetime.datetime) -> list[str]:
"""Again presses per answer in the SETTLE_DAYS before each proposal and after its fix, for the
fixes that changed a note's fields and have had that long to show."""
window = datetime.timedelta(days=SETTLE_DAYS)
settled = [
state for state in states
if state["status"] == "applied" and state.get("action") in FIELD_ACTIONS and state.get("cardIds")
and now - parse_stamp(state["closedAt"]) >= window
if not settled:
return ["No field fix has had %d days to show its effect yet." % SETTLE_DAYS]
if not connected():
return ["Anki is closed, so what the applied fixes changed was not measured."]
logs = review_logs(sorted({card for state in settled for card in state["cardIds"]}))
lines = ["| Check | Fixes | Again before | Again after |", "| --- | --- | --- | --- |"]
for kind in KINDS:
mine = [state for state in settled if state["kind"] == kind]
if not mine:
continue
tally = {"before": [0, 0], "after": [0, 0]}
for state in mine:
proposed, fixed = parse_stamp(state["at"]), parse_stamp(state["closedAt"])
spans = {"before": (proposed - window, proposed), "after": (fixed, fixed + window)}
for card in state["cardIds"]:
for entry in logs.get(card, []):
moment = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(entry["id"] / 1000, datetime.timezone.utc)
for side, (start, end) in spans.items():
if start <= moment < end:
tally[side][0] += entry["ease"] == AGAIN
tally[side][1] += 1
lines.append("| %s | %d | %s | %s |" % (kind, len(mine), share(*tally["before"]), share(*tally["after"])))
return lines
def cmd_queue_report(args) -> int:

states = proposal_states(records)

since = now - datetime.timedelta(days=args.days)
lines = [
"# Repair queue, %s" % now.date(),
"The last %d days of %s." % (args.days, path),
"| Check | Checked | Needed a change | Accepted | Pending | Runs without Anki | Last run |",
for kind in KINDS:
recent = [state for state in states if state["kind"] == kind and parse_stamp(state["at"]) >= since]
changes = [state for state in recent if state["action"] != "keep"]
decided = [state for state in changes if state["status"] in VERDICTS]
applied = sum(1 for state in decided if state["status"] == "applied")
waiting = sum(1 for state in changes if state["status"] == "pending")
missed = sum(1 for record in skips if record.get("kind") == kind and parse_stamp(record["at"]) >= since)
last = max([state["at"] for state in states if state["kind"] == kind]
+ [record["at"] for record in skips if record.get("kind") == kind], default="")
lines.append("| %s | %d | %s | %s | %d | %d | %s |" % (
kind, len(recent), share(len(changes), len(recent)), share(applied, len(decided)), waiting, missed,
last[:10] or "never"))
lines += ["", "## What the fixes changed", ""] + fix_effects(states, now)
text = "\n".join(lines)
print(text)
if args.save:
out = path.parent / "reports" / ("%s.md" % now.date().isoformat())
out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
out.write_text(text + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
print("\nSaved to %s." % out)
return 0
